column1: Schopenhauer — the fourfold root: reconstruct the argument that the principle of sufficient reason has exactly four forms, and state the error he accuses earlier philosophy of.
column2:
1. Every representation stands under the principle: nothing is without a reason why it is so.
2. The principle's form varies with the class of object: causes for material objects (becoming), logical grounds for judgments (knowing), mutual determination in space and time (being), motives for actions (acting).
3. Therefore no single form may be applied outside its class.
Objection: the fourfold scheme is stipulative taxonomy.
Reply: it does diagnostic work — the classic confusions (treating grounds as causes, motives as causes of a free will) are exactly crossings of the classes.

column1: Schopenhauer — the world as representation: reconstruct the argument, including what he keeps from Kant and what he discards.
column2:
1. The world as experienced is representation: an object for a subject, structured a priori by space, time, and causality.
2. These forms belong to the knowing subject, so the experienced world is appearance, not things as they are in themselves (Kant's result, kept).
3. But Kant's machinery is bloated: causality alone does the understanding's work, and the categories collapse into it (Kant, corrected).
Objection: this is Berkeleyan subjectivism.
Reply: representations are law-governed and shared in form; and representation is only half the story — Book 2 supplies the other.

column1: Schopenhauer — the body's double knowledge: reconstruct the argument that the thing-in-itself is Will, and name its weakest joint.
column2:
1. My body is given twice over: as representation among representations, and immediately, from within, as willing — desire, striving, aversion.
2. This inner side is not itself a representation; it is the one place where a phenomenon is known as it is in itself.
3. Generalizing: every phenomenon has such an inner side, and it is the same in kind — Will, at different grades.
Objection: step 3 is an analogy dressed as a deduction.
Reply: the alternative leaves one's own case a miracle; but the joint is real, and the literature still fights over it.

column1: Schopenhauer — individuation: explain how the one Will becomes many competing individuals, and why the explanation matters ethically.
column2:
1. The Will in itself is one, outside space and time.
2. Space and time are forms of representation — the principium individuationis: through them the one Will appears as a plurality of individuals in space and time.
3. Each individual takes itself to be the whole Will and treats others as mere representations, so egoism and conflict are built into appearance.
Objection: if plurality is mere appearance, why does suffering matter?
Reply: suffering belongs to appearance, but appearance is the only world sufferers have; the ethics of Book 4 works at exactly that level.

column1: Schopenhauer — striving and suffering: reconstruct the pessimism argument from willing to the pendulum of pain and boredom.
column2:
1. Willing springs from lack, deficiency — and lack is suffering.
2. Satisfaction is purely negative: it merely silences one want, briefly, and spawns new wants.
3. If no want comes, boredom — itself a torment — takes its place.
4. Therefore life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom, and suffering is the structure of willing, not an accident of bad arrangements.
Objection: joys are positive, not mere absences of pain.
Reply: we feel pain positively and health only negatively — we notice the shoe that pinches, never the one that fits.

column1: Schopenhauer — the worst of all possible worlds: state the argument and what it is meant to answer.
column2:
1. Leibniz: this is the best of all possible worlds.
2. Schopenhauer's inversion: a world even a little worse in its basic arrangement could not continue to exist at all — its miseries would destroy it.
3. Therefore this world is the worst that is compatible with continued existence: as bad as a world can be while still being.
Objection: this trades on 'possible' meaning 'sustainable,' which begs the question.
Reply: granted in part — the argument is a rebuttal inside Leibniz's own terms, aimed at optimism, not a free-standing proof of pessimism.

column1: Schopenhauer — compassion: reconstruct the argument that Mitleid is the sole basis of morality, and the metaphysics it depends on.
column2:
1. Actions have moral worth only when they aim at another's weal for its own sake.
2. This happens only in compassion: I suffer another's suffering as mine, because the barrier between self and other falls.
3. That barrier is individuation — appearance only; in himself the other is the same Will I am.
4. Therefore compassion, not duty or command, is morality's genuine source.
Objection: step 3 makes ethics hostage to a disputed metaphysics.
Reply (Shapshay's line): the phenomenology of compassion may stand on thinner grounds — the debate is live.

column1: Schopenhauer — aesthetic release: reconstruct the argument that art temporarily frees us from the Will.
column2:
1. Ordinary knowing serves the will: it asks where, when, and why — relations under the principle of sufficient reason.
2. In aesthetic contemplation we rest in perception of the Platonic Idea and stop asking those questions; we become the pure subject of knowing.
3. For as long as it lasts, desire and its suffering are suspended — we are delivered from the penal servitude of willing.
Objection: a release that ends when the concert ends is no solution.
Reply: agreed — it is proof of concept, not salvation; Book 4 seeks the permanent version.

column1: Schopenhauer — music: state his claim for music's unique rank among the arts, and the tension it creates in the system.
column2:
Claim: the other arts copy the Platonic Ideas — the Will's adequate objectifications, grade by grade. Music bypasses the Ideas entirely: it is a direct copy of the Will itself, which is why its effect is so much more powerful and immediate than any image of the world.
Tension: the system's architecture routes all art through the Ideas; music's directness is an anomaly. Schopenhauer asserts the exception more than he explains it.
Use the tension, do not hide it: capstone material.

column1: Schopenhauer — denial of the will: reconstruct the final step of Book 4, and explain why suicide is its opposite.
column2:
1. Knowledge of the whole — that willing is suffering and individuation illusion — can become a quietive of the will itself.
2. The will then turns against itself: denial of the will-to-live, seen outwardly as asceticism, resignation, holiness.
3. Suicide is the opposite phenomenon: the suicide wills life and rejects only its sufferings, destroying one appearance while affirming willing — a paradoxical affirmation.
Objection: who performs the denial, if the denier is an individuated appearance?
Reply: the will itself, through knowledge — a reply many readers judge a mystery relabeled.

column1: Schopenhauer — freedom and character: reconstruct operari sequitur esse and say what freedom survives it.
column2:
1. A person's acts follow necessarily from motives acting on his character: action follows being — operari sequitur esse.
2. The empirical character is inborn and unchangeable, so no act could have been otherwise, given the motive.
3. Freedom is not thereby abolished but relocated: the intelligible character is a timeless act of will outside appearance, and responsibility attaches there.
Objection: a freedom located where nothing can change is freedom in name only.
Reply: it explains the datum — we blame the person, not the act — which is what the theory was built to save.

column1: Schopenhauer — eternal justice: state the doctrine and distinguish it from retribution after death.
column2:
1. The Will is one; tormentor and tormented are the same Will appearing under individuation, at odds with itself.
2. Therefore the world's suffering is exactly the Will's self-torment, and justice needs no future tribunal: it is already executed in the structure of things — eternal, not postponed.
3. Guilt attaches to existence itself: to be an individual appearance of the Will is already to share in its deed.
Objection: this consoles no victim and accuses every sufferer.
Reply: it is a metaphysical identity claim, not a courtroom verdict on persons — but the discomfort is the standing objection.

column1: Schopenhauer — primacy of will over intellect: reconstruct the argument that intellect is the will's tool.
column2:
1. Self-observation shows the intellect learning the will's decisions only after the fact, and routinely manufacturing reasons for them (rationalization).
2. Desire regularly defeats known better judgment; attention, memory, and mood all bend toward what we want.
3. Conclusion: intellect is secondary — an instrument the will uses, as claws and teeth are instruments, not the self's sovereign part.
Objection: intellect can also overrule desire, as in ascetic knowledge (Book 4).
Reply: precisely — and Schopenhauer needs that exception; his name for it is the intellect outgrowing its office.

column1: Explain Vorstellung (representation) in Schopenhauer's usage, and what it excludes.
column2: Vorstellung is anything as it exists for a subject: the experienced world in its entirety, structured by the a priori forms of space, time, and causality. To call the world representation is not to call it illusion or private fantasy — its order is lawful and common. The term excludes exactly one thing: the world as it is in itself, apart from being known — which Book 2 approaches from inside, through the body, as Will.

column1: Define the principle of sufficient reason and its fourfold root, in one card.
column2: The principle: nothing is without a reason why it is so and not otherwise. The root is fourfold because the reason differs by class of object: cause (becoming — why this state followed that one), logical ground (knowing — why this judgment is true), ground in space and time (being — why these positions and magnitudes), motive (acting — why this deed, given this character). The dissertation's policing rule: never answer a question of one class with a reason of another.

column1: Define the principium individuationis — and what falls with it in compassion and in death.
column2: Space and time, the forms through which the one Will appears as a plurality of separate individuals. It is 'principle' in the sense of source: individuation, egoism, and conflict all originate here. In compassion the principle is seen through — the other is felt as oneself. In death it simply lapses for the individual: the appearance ends, the Will it appeared as does not.

column1: Define the Will (capital W) so that it cannot be confused with willpower.
column2: The Will is the thing-in-itself of the world: one, timeless, aimless striving without purpose or final satisfaction, objectifying itself in gravity and magnetism as much as in animal appetite and human ambition. Willpower — deliberate, motive-guided choosing — is one of its individuated appearances, late and local. The Will is not a person, not a god, not under your ego's control; your ego is one of its splinters, set against the others.

column1: What are the grades of objectification, and what are the Platonic Ideas doing in this system?
column2: The Will objectifies itself at fixed grades, from blind natural forces through plant and animal life to human willing. Schopenhauer identifies these grades with Plato's Ideas: eternal forms, known not by abstraction but in will-less perception. They are the middle storey of the system — the Will itself above, individual things below — and the arts are ranked by the grade their objects embody, which is why architecture sits lowest and, music excepted, poetry highest.

column1: Define the body as 'immediate object' and state why the system cannot start anywhere else.
column2: Every other object is known only as representation, mediated by the forms of knowing. The body alone is also known immediately, from within, as willing — acts of will and movements of the body are one and the same, given in two ways. It is the system's single keyhole: the only point where representation and thing-in-itself coincide in one item, and therefore the only possible starting point for the inference to the Will in all nature.

column1: Define the pure subject of knowing, and its relation to genius.
column2: The state in which a knower has forgotten his own will, his body, and his interests, and rests wholly in the perception of an object — subject and object both purified of striving. Ordinary people touch it for moments, in art and in nature. Genius is the capacity to sustain it: an excess of intellect beyond what the individual's will needs, turned loose on the Ideas — which is why genius, for Schopenhauer, is kin to madness and useless for practical life.

column1: Distinguish the beautiful from the sublime in Schopenhauer's aesthetics.
column2: Both are will-less contemplation of Ideas. In the beautiful, the object invites it: form pleases, the will falls silent without resistance. In the sublime, the object is felt as hostile to the will — vast, threatening, indifferent — and the contemplative state must be won by consciously tearing oneself away from that relation. The sublime is therefore the beautiful plus an effort, and its pleasure carries an undertone of exaltation at the will's defeat.

column1: Define Mitleid and give its three expressions in conduct.
column2: Mitleid — compassion, literally suffering-with — is the immediate participation in another's suffering such that the distinction between self and other no longer governs one's action. Schopenhauer treats it as an original phenomenon, not derivable from egoism. In conduct it appears in three descending grades: it restrains harm (justice — injure no one), it moves to positive help (loving-kindness — help everyone as much as you can), and at its limit it issues in resignation, the denial of the will itself.

column1: Distinguish intelligible, empirical, and acquired character.
column2: Intelligible character: what a person is in himself — the will's timeless, unchangeable act, outside appearance. Empirical character: that same character unfolded in time, knowable only a posteriori, through the person's deeds; motives act on it with necessity. Acquired character: not a third thing but the self-knowledge, won through experience, of which empirical character one has — learning to will only what one's character can actually achieve. It is the only self-improvement the system permits.

column1: Define denial of the will-to-live — and what it is not.
column2: The will, through complete knowledge of its own nature, ceases to affirm itself: desire quiets, then is renounced, in asceticism, chastity, voluntary poverty — the state Schopenhauer finds described in Christian sainthood, Hindu renunciation, and Buddhism alike. It is not suicide (which affirms willing while rejecting its sufferings), not depression (a state of thwarted willing), and not a technique: in his account it arrives through knowledge and suffering, more like grace than like a decision.

column1: State Schopenhauer's pessimism in one precise sentence, and the sentence to never confuse it with.
column2: Precise: because the essence of everything is a willing that springs from lack and can be satisfied only negatively and briefly, suffering is a structural feature of existence, and nonexistence would be preferable to existence. Never confuse it with: 'Schopenhauer was a gloomy man who thought life usually goes badly.' The first is a metaphysical argument that would stand even if its author had been cheerful; the second is biography, and does no philosophical work.

column1: Define the will-to-live (Wille zum Leben) and its relation to the Will.
column2: The will-to-live is the Will as it appears in living nature: the striving to exist, persist, and reproduce that runs from an animal's self-preservation to the whole machinery of sexual love, in which the species' interest overrides the individual's happiness. It is not a second entity alongside the Will but the Will named at the grade of life — and it is the specific target of denial: what the saint denies is not an abstraction but this striving in himself.

column1: Define eternal justice without using the word 'punishment.'
column2: The doctrine that the world's moral accounts are already balanced within existence itself: because tormentor and tormented are one and the same Will under the illusion of separateness, the suffering of the world is the Will's own deed against itself, and no afterlife tribunal is needed to set it right. Its corollary is inherited guilt of a metaphysical kind: the offense is existence as an individuated appearance, not any particular act — which is why critics find it profound and outrageous in equal measure.

column1: What is the 'quietive' of the will, and why does the system need the concept?
column2: A quietive is knowledge that does not merely inform the will but silences it: the insight into individuation and suffering, when it becomes complete and constant, acts on willing as a motive acts — but in reverse, stilling instead of spurring. The system needs the concept because Book 4's turn is otherwise impossible: motives can only produce more willing, so if liberation is to happen at all, knowledge must be able to function in this second, opposed way. Whether it can is one of the system's standing disputes.

column1: Define acquired character's practical payoff: what can a person actually change, on Schopenhauer's account?
column2: Nothing about what he is: the empirical character is fixed, and resolutions addressed to it fail exactly as he predicts. What can change is aim. Acquired character — accurate knowledge of one's own fixed strengths, weaknesses, and desires — lets a person stop willing what his character cannot reach and concentrate on what it can, trading a life of self-reproach for a deliberate one. It is the whole content of the practical wisdom in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life.
